title: On the phone
job: Calls and messages — openings, closings, taking a message
verifiedBy: Claude Opus 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: man is "who" and min is "from", and they differ by one short vowel. Short vowels are always written in this course for exactly this reason: min maʿī would send a learner to a note about origins.

laysa negates a sentence that has no verb — huwa laysa mawjūd — where lā negates a verb. L1 kept it out on purpose; a phone call's whole business is absence, so this level lifts it in the third person only.
ālū is what every Arabic speaker says on picking up. It came in from the French and there is no MSA alternative anybody uses, so it is written like any other word.
bi- takes the suffixes like any preposition: bika to a man, biki to a woman. sa-attaṣil bika is "I will contact you", and the verb needs the bi- to reach its object.

words.note: From the French, and used on every Arabic phone. There is no MSA rival anybody says, so the course writes it like any other word.
One short vowel from M1's min, "from", and identical to it in the Arabic line — من for both. The written vowel in the romanization is the only thing keeping them apart.

sentences.trap: man and min are the same three letters in Arabic. This course writes every short vowel precisely so that the romanized line can tell them apart, and this is the sentence that pays for that decision.
sentences.sound: ā-LŪ, and MAN with a short a — the vowel is the whole word.

variations.changed: asking for someone rather than asking who called
min and man in one sentence, a vowel apart
the caller identifying themselves

mistake.why: min is "from". The question is man maʿī — and the Arabic line will not warn you, because both are من.

sentences.usage: Answering a call from a number you do not know. maʿī is literally "with me", which is how Arabic asks who is on the line.
sentences.mnemonic: One vowel between who and from.

words.note: An adjective meaning present or available, agreeing with the person asked after. mawjūd for a man.

sentences.trap: No verb, and no word for "is". Asking whether someone is in is a nominal sentence like every other one in this course.
sentences.sound: maw-JŪ-da, with the aw as in "how" and the stress on the long ū.

variations.changed: a man, so the adjective drops its -a
a role instead of a name
the answer, with M2's hiya

mistake.why: Hind is a woman, so the adjective is mawjūda. It agrees with the person, as every adjective in this course does.

sentences.usage: Calling a house or an office. It is the question the whole module is built around.
sentences.mnemonic: Present is an adjective, so it belongs to whoever is present.

words.note: Negates a sentence with no verb in it, which lā cannot do. This course teaches only the third person — laysa and laysat — and the rest of the paradigm waits.
Always written with al-, and the madda over the alif marks a long ā. It never appears without the article.

sentences.trap: lā will not do this job. lā negates a verb, and there is no verb here — which is exactly why L1 had no way to say it and this module needs a new word.
sentences.sound: LAY-sa, and al-ĀN with a long open ā.

variations.changed: the feminine, in both words

mistake.why: lā needs a verb to negate. A sentence with none takes laysa.

sentences.usage: What an office says fifty times a day. The offer in the third variation is what should follow it.
sentences.mnemonic: No verb to negate, so lā has nothing to hold on to.

words.note: The feminine of laysa, and here the Arabic line SHOWS the difference — ليست against ليس — unlike M1's samaḥta and samaḥti. The row for laysa is S03's.

sentences.trap: Two words agree with her and both change. The negator itself is one of them, which no other word in this course does.

sentences.usage: The same answer about a woman. Notice that the script distinguishes these two and did not distinguish M1's pair.
sentences.mnemonic: Even the negation has a gender.

words.note: tarak, to leave something behind — not to leave a place. The ta- prefix is "you", the same one in tadhhab and tashrab.
Feminine. It covers a spoken message, a letter and a text alike, so the sentence says which.

sentences.trap: M1's frame, unchanged, on a new verb. Nothing about the politeness is new — only the thing being asked.
sentences.sound: ri-SĀ-la, with the stress on the long ā.

sentences.usage: Offered by whoever answered, and the polite thing to offer when the person is out.

sentences.cue: Do you have the phone number?

words.note: The first noun of a two-noun possession, so it takes no al- even though the phrase is definite — M2's iḍāfa rule, on the phone.
The MSA word for a phone. Every country has its own everyday one — mobile, jawwāl, telifūn — and this course writes al-hātif and names the others nowhere else.

sentences.trap: raqm al-hātif is one possession, so only the second word takes al-. M2's iḍāfa rule, and this is the phrase where a learner meets it most often.
sentences.sound: RAQM, one syllable with the q at the back. al-HĀ-tif.

variations.cue: Do you have the phone number? (to a woman)

mistake.why: The first noun of a possession never takes al-: raqm al-hātif. With al- on both, the phrase falls apart.

sentences.usage: Everyday. The second variation is the shape you will hear more often, with the person's own suffix on the end.
sentences.mnemonic: Only the owner takes the al-.

words.note: To make contact, and it needs bi- to reach the person contacted. sa- in front is M6's future from the level below.
M4's bi- taking the possessive suffixes, exactly as ʿind- does. biki to a woman, and the Arabic line writes both as بك.

sentences.trap: The verb cannot reach its object without bi-. attaṣil ka is not a sentence; the preposition is part of the verb's shape.
sentences.sound: sa-at-ta-ṢIL, with the ṣ emphatic and the t doubled.

mistake.why: The verb takes bi-: sa-attaṣil bika. And a pronoun never stands alone in Arabic — it glues on.

sentences.usage: How every Arabic phone call ends when it has not finished its business.
sentences.mnemonic: The verb reaches its person through a preposition.

words.note: One word, and it holds the line. Both the ḥ and the ẓ are made deep — the ẓ is an emphatic dh, and the word is unmistakable because of it.

sentences.trap: No verb, no article, and it is complete. Arabic hands over the noun and the politeness and nothing else.
sentences.sound: LAḤ-ẓa, with the ḥ a hard breath and the ẓ dark and emphatic.

sentences.usage: On a phone, at a counter, in a doorway. It buys as much time as it needs to.
sentences.mnemonic: A moment is not a particular moment.

words.note: M6's row from the level below, and it covers a busy person and a busy line alike. The row is L1-M6's; this module only re-shows it.

sentences.trap: The same word does the person and the line. Arabic makes no distinction English speakers expect between being busy and being engaged.
sentences.sound: mash-GHŪL, with the gh a soft gargled g and the stress on the long ū.

sentences.usage: The other reason someone cannot come to the phone. Between this and S03 the module covers both.
sentences.mnemonic: Busy is a state, and a state needs no verb.

words.note: M10's phrase from the level below, and the standard way to end a call. Arabic's goodbye is about the next meeting rather than this parting.

sentences.trap: Nothing new in the whole sentence, and that is the point of a module's last rung: it should be recombination.

sentences.usage: The end of the call. maʿa as-salāma is what the other person says back, which is why both are in the variations.
sentences.mnemonic: Every Arabic goodbye is an appointment.
